warmup.q: record Masked(String phone) overrides its accessor so that phone() returns "****0123" for the number 01614960123. What does toString() return?
options: Nothing: it doesn't compile, because record accessors can't be overridden
Masked@1b6d3586, because overriding an accessor turns off the generated toString
warmup.why: The generated toString, equals and hashCode read the private field directly, not the accessor, so the full number reaches the log. Overriding an accessor is legal as long as the return type matches. To hide a component, override toString itself, as the lab does. The section on equality and immutability shows it with real output.

opening:
Picture the front desk of a small town library. To borrow books, you fill in a loan slip: your member number, the titles, and the date they're due back. It sits in a clear sleeve, so anyone can read every box, and nothing is written on the back. Two slips filled in the same way stand for the same loan. Before a slip is stamped, the clerk at the counter checks it.

Programs are full of slips like that: small classes that only carry data. For years Java made you write them by hand: fields, a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode and toString. That's five places that must agree on what the data is, and nothing makes them agree. Someone adds a box and updates three places out of five, and the program quietly treats two different slips as one.

The design patterns track was about objects that carry behavior. This track is about the data they carry. In this lesson, we'll let a record write those five places from one line, give it a counter where every instance is checked, and find where its promises stop. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the front desk, with a loan slip in a clear sleeve. A record is that slip, and its components are the boxes. javac writes what we used to keep in five places, and the compact constructor is the counter every instance passes, whichever door it came through. Its promises stop one level down, at the attached list and the masked accessor.

Now look in your own code for a class with equals, hashCode and toString written by hand. Compare the fields each one uses. If the three lists differ, you've found a drifting form.

Next, we'll fix which kinds of form exist at all. How can the compiler know it has seen every kind of library item?

sections.h: A record is its components, and javac writes the rest
sections.html:
Start with a shelfmark, the label on a book's spine that says where the book lives: a three-letter section and a shelf number, such as FIC 12. Here it is the way Java classes were written for years, by hand. The shelf number was added later:

Java
public final class Shelfmark {
    private final String section;
    private final int shelf;                         // added later

    public Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { this.section = section; this.shelf = shelf; }
    public String section() { return section; }
    public int shelf() { return shelf; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Shelfmark s && s.section.equals(section);   // nobody updated this
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return section.hashCode(); }
    @Override public String toString() { return "Shelfmark[section=" + section + "]"; }
}
Kotlin
class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) {               // shelf added later
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Shelfmark && other.section == section   // nobody updated this
    override fun hashCode() = section.hashCode()
    override fun toString() = "Shelfmark(section=$section)"
}

It compiles. The RecordAnatomy demo in the Try it keeps this class as OldShelfmark and runs it on two books on different shelves:

by hand:    OldShelfmark[section=FIC] equals OldShelfmark[section=FIC]: true

Shelf 12 and shelf 40 now count as the same place, and the log line can't even say which shelf it meant. The class states "these fields are the data" in five places: the fields, the constructor, equals, hashCode and toString. Five copies of one list drifted apart, the way paperwork does when nobody owns it.

A record states it once. A record is a class whose header lists its components, the values that make up its data, and javac, the Java compiler, writes everything else from that list:

Java
public record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) {}
Kotlin
data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int)

Here is the picture we'll use for the whole track: library paperwork. A record is a filled-in form in a clear sleeve. Each component is one box on the form, and what you see through the sleeve is all there is: no notes on the back, no hidden boxes. Comparing two forms means comparing them box by box. Reading a form aloud means reading every box, in order.

javac turns that one line into the parts we used to type. Each component gets a private final field and a public accessor, a method named after the component that returns it: section() and shelf(), with no get. The canonical constructor takes every component, in header order. equals, hashCode and toString use every component, so they can't drift. The class is final and extends java.lang.Record. Records have been a final feature, that is, finished and switched on, since JDK 16 (JEP 395, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that describes them). So all of this works on the JDK 21 the labs compile for.

Five copies of one list drift apart. Write the list once, in the header.

The Record Javadoc calls a record "a shallowly immutable, transparent carrier for a fixed set of values", and each word is a rule. Fixed: you can't add instance fields, and private int cache; in the body fails with field declaration must be static. Static fields, methods and nested types are fine. Transparent: the state is the API, so every component is public through its accessor. A record can implement interfaces, but it can't extend a class, because it already extends Record. Shallowly immutable gets its own section below.

The generated methods aren't what you would write by hand, and you can see that one level down. javap, the JDK's class-file reader, shows that equals, hashCode and toString are each one invokedynamic instruction. That is a call whose target the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, picks the first time the call runs, by asking a bootstrap method, here ObjectMethods.bootstrap. javac hands it the component names as one string, section;shelf, and a getter for each private field, and the JDK builds the method bodies from that list. That's why the Javadoc says the toString format may change: never parse it. kotlinc, the Kotlin compiler, does it the older way and writes the bodies into your class.

A record is still an ordinary object with its own identity: every new makes a separate one. Two forms with the same boxes are still two sheets of paper, so new Shelfmark("FIC", 12) == new Shelfmark("FIC", 12) is false, and synchronized on a record works. Objects without identity are what Project Valhalla adds, as a preview in JDK 28 (a preview feature is switched off unless you ask for it, and may still change). Lesson 4 of this track covers it.

javac now prints every box on the form. It doesn't yet check what anybody writes in them.

try.title: Look inside a record
steps: Run RecordAnatomy (or its Kotlin twin) with the command below. Predict the == line before you look.
From labs/, print the bytecode of the nested record: javap -p -c 'modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/RecordAnatomy$Shelfmark.class'. Find the three invokedynamic lines.

code.title: RecordAnatomy.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.Arrays; /** What javac gives a one-line record, seen from the outside. */ public class RecordAnatomy { // Naive: written by hand. The shelf was added later, and not to every method. static final class OldShelfmark { private final String section; private final int shelf; // added later OldShelfmark(String section, int shelf) { this.section = section; this.shelf = shelf; } String section() { return section; } int shelf() { return shelf; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof OldShelfmark s && s.section.equals(section); // nobody updated this } @Override public int hashCode() { return section.hashCode(); } @Override public String toString() { return "OldShelfmark[section=" + section + "]"; } } record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) {} public static void main(String[] args) { OldShelfmark old12 = new OldShelfmark("FIC", 12), old40 = new OldShelfmark("FIC", 40); System.out.println("by hand: " + old12 + " equals " + old40 + ": " + old12.equals(old40)); Shelfmark a = new Shelfmark("FIC", 12); Shelfmark b = new Shelfmark("FIC", 12); System.out.println("toString: " + a); System.out.println("accessors: section()=" + a.section() + " shelf()=" + a.shelf()); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", same hashCode: " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode())); System.out.println("==: " + (a == b) + " (two objects, each with its own identity)"); System.out.println("isRecord: " + Shelfmark.class.isRecord()); System.out.println("components: " + Arrays.toString(Shelfmark.class.getRecordComponents())); System.out.println("superclass: " + Shelfmark.class.getSuperclass().getName()); synchronized (a) { // compiles and runs: a record is an ordinary identity object System.out.println("locked on a record"); } } }

try.expect: The first line shows the hand-written class calling two different shelves equal: OldShelfmark[section=FIC] equals OldShelfmark[section=FIC]: true. Then the record prints Shelfmark[section=FIC, shelf=12], equals: true, ==: false, isRecord: true and the components [java.lang.String section, int shelf]. The Kotlin twin prints isRecord: false for the plain data class and true for the @JvmRecord one. In the javap -v output, the bootstrap method is ObjectMethods.bootstrap, and its arguments include the string section;shelf and two REF_getField handles on the private fields. The Kotlin class has getSection(), component1(), copy(java.lang.String, int) and copy$default(...) instead.

aside.title: Can a component have any name?
aside.html: Almost any. The Java Language Specification forbids eight: clone, finalize, getClass, hashCode, notify, notifyAll, toString and wait. Each one would give the record an accessor with the same name as a method of Object, so javac stops with illegal record component name wait. A plain Kotlin data class turns val wait into getWait(), so the clash doesn't come up there. In Java, a waiting time is expectedWait, which reads better anyway.

video.title: A record is a form in a clear sleeve: javac writes every method from one list, the compact constructor checks every copy, and the promise stops at the attached list

sections.h: The compact constructor: one counter every instance passes
sections.html:
A form is only as good as the counter that checks it. Suppose the checks live in a static factory, Shelfmark.of(...). It can check the section all it likes, and new Shelfmark("fiction!", -3) walks straight past it, through the side door.

A record gives you a counter with no side door. Every other constructor must call the canonical constructor first, with this(...), and so does every factory and every wither. That makes the canonical constructor the one place to check and tidy every instance. You write it in the compact form, with no parameter list:

Java
record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) {
    Shelfmark {                                          // the compact canonical constructor
        Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section");
        if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("shelf must be 1 or more: " + shelf);
        section = section.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);      // reassign the parameter
    }                                                    // javac assigns the fields here

    Shelfmark(String section) { this(section, 1); }     // any other constructor calls it first
}
Kotlin
data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) {
    init {                                               // runs on every construction, and on copy()
        require(shelf >= 1) { "shelf must be 1 or more: $shelf" }
        require(section == section.uppercase()) { "section must be upper case: $section" }
    }

    constructor(section: String) : this(section, 1)     // any other constructor calls it first
}

Read the compact constructor as the clerk at the counter. First it rejects a missing section, then it checks the shelf, and finally it tidies the writing, so "fic" becomes "FIC". In the compact form the parameters are ordinary local variables. You may reassign them, and javac copies their final values into the fields after your code runs. The clerk can't stamp the fields directly: this.shelf = shelf; fails with cannot assign a value to final variable shelf.

The second constructor shows the rule for side doors: it must start with this(section, 1). On JDK 21, any statement before that line fails with constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Shelfmark. JDK 25 made flexible constructor bodies final (JEP 513), so there you may run plain statements first, such as splitting the label "fic 12" in two, as long as they don't touch the fields.

The Kotlin twin shows a real difference. init runs on every construction, including copy(). But a data class can't change a constructor parameter before it becomes a property. It can reject "fic", but it can't turn it into "FIC". Tidying moves into a factory function, and the public constructor still accepts the raw value.

The last door is deserialization, which rebuilds an object from bytes, for example bytes read back from a file. The Record Javadoc says the canonical constructor runs during deserialization, so a record gets its checks there for free. An ordinary class needs a hand-written readObject method to check itself again, and most classes don't have one. A Kotlin data class doesn't run its init there at all, unless it's marked @JvmRecord, which compiles it to a real record.

The demo in the Try it swaps two numbers inside the bytes of a PageRange, a request to photocopy pages 1 to 5, and reads it back. The Java record prints tampered stream rejected: first > last: 5 > 1. The Kotlin twin prints:

tampered stream gave: PageRangeK(first=5, last=1)
tampered stream rejected: first > last: 5 > 1

The plain data class climbed in through a window: it came back as a range its own init forbids. The @JvmRecord version went past the clerk like everyone else.

A check that some paths skip is only a suggestion. Put it in the canonical constructor.

The clerk checks what's written in every box. The clerk can't see a sheet stapled to the form that somebody is still writing on.

code.title: CompactConstructorDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream; import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream; import java.io.ObjectInputStream; import java.io.ObjectOutputStream; import java.io.Serializable; import java.util.Locale; import java.util.Objects; /** Every way of making a record goes through its canonical constructor, even deserialization. */ public class CompactConstructorDemo { record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { Shelfmark { // compact canonical constructor Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section"); if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("shelf must be 1 or more: " + shelf); section = section.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // reassign the parameter } // fields are assigned here Shelfmark(String section) { this(section, 1); } // non-canonical: must delegate static Shelfmark parse(String label) { // a factory: still goes through it String[] parts = label.trim().split(" "); return new Shelfmark(parts[0], Integer.parseInt(parts[1])); } } // a request to photocopy pages first to last of a book record PageRange(int first, int last) implements Serializable { PageRange { if (first > last) throw new IllegalArgumentException("first > last: " + first + " > " + last); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(new Shelfmark("fic", 12)); System.out.println(new Shelfmark("bio")); System.out.println(Shelfmark.parse("ref 7")); try { new Shelfmark("FIC", 0); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("IAE: " + e.getMessage()); } try { new Shelfmark(null, 1); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NPE: " + e.getMessage()); } // serialize a valid PageRange, then swap its two int fields in the byte stream byte[] bytes = serialize(new PageRange(1, 5)); swapLastTwoInts(bytes); try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes))) { System.out.println("tampered stream gave: " + in.readObject()); } catch (java.io.InvalidObjectException e) { System.out.println("tampered stream rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } } static byte[] serialize(Object o) throws Exception { var buf = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); try (var out = new ObjectOutputStream(buf)) { out.writeObject(o); } return buf.toByteArray(); } // the stream ends with the two int fields; swapping them turns (1, 5) into (5, 1) static void swapLastTwoInts(byte[] b) { int n = b.length; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { byte t = b[n - 8 + i]; b[n - 8 + i] = b[n - 4 + i]; b[n - 4 + i] = t; } } }

normalizing happens in a factory instead. data class SpineLabel(val section: String, val shelf: Int) { init { require(shelf >= 1) { "shelf must be 1 or more: $shelf" } require(section == section.uppercase()) { "section must be upper case: $section" } } constructor(section: String) : this(section, 1) // secondary: must delegate companion object { fun of(section: String, shelf: Int) = class PageRangeK(val first: Int, val last: Int) : Serializable { init { require(first <= last) { "first > last: $first > $last" } } } @JvmRecord // a real JVM record data class PageRangeR(val first: Int, val last: Int) : Serializable { init { require(first <= last) { "first > last: $first > $last" } } } /** Every way of making a data class runs init... except Java deserialization of a plain data class. */ fun main() { println(SpineLabel.of("fic", 12)) println(SpineLabel("BIO")) println(SpineLabel.parse("ref 7")) try { SpineLabel("FIC", 0) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("IAE: ${e.message}") } for (range in listOf<Any>(PageRangeK(1, 5), PageRangeR(1, 5))) { val bytes = serialize(range) swapLastTwoInts(bytes) try { val back = ObjectInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)).use { it.readObject() } println("tampered stream gave: $back") } catch (e: InvalidObjectException) { println("tampered stream rejected: ${e.message}") } } } private fun serialize(o: Any): ByteArray { val buf = ByteArrayOutputStream() ObjectOutputStream(buf).use { it.writeObject(o) } return buf.toByteArray() } // the stream ends with the two int fields; swapping them turns (1, 5) into (5, 1) private fun swapLastTwoInts(b: ByteArray) { val n = b.size for (i in 0 until 4) { val t = b[n - 8 + i] b[n - 8 + i] = b[n - 4 + i] b[n - 4 + i] = t } }

try.expect: The Java demo prints Shelfmark[section=FIC, shelf=12], Shelfmark[section=BIO, shelf=1], Shelfmark[section=REF, shelf=7], IAE: shelf must be 1 or more: 0, NPE: section and finally tampered stream rejected: first > last: 5 > 1. Deserialization called the compact constructor, it threw, and ObjectInputStream wrapped that in an InvalidObjectException. The Kotlin twin prints tampered stream gave: PageRangeK(first=5, last=1) for the plain data class, an object its own init forbids, and rejects the @JvmRecord one. The field assignment fails with cannot assign a value to final variable shelf. On JDK 25 the preview file reads fic 12 into Shelfmark[section=FIC, shelf=12]. JDK 21 rejects it with constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Shelfmark and call to this must be first statement in constructor.

sections.h: Equality and immutability go one level deep
sections.html:
Start with what equals compares. Two records are equal when they're the same record class and every component is equal. For a reference component that means Objects.equals. For a primitive it means the wrapper's compare method returns 0, which holds two surprises for a double. A record holding NaN, the "not a number" value, equals another one holding NaN, though NaN == NaN is false. And records holding 0.0 and -0.0 aren't equal, though 0.0 == -0.0 is true. Kotlin data classes behave the same way.

Arrays are worse. An int[] component compares by reference, so two records with equal arrays aren't equal, and toString prints something like [I@1b6d3586. Use a List instead.

A List component brings the real trap. Picture a form with a box that says "see attached list", and a list stapled behind it. The form is checked and stamped, but whoever kept a copy of the attached sheet can still write on it. A record holds a reference to whatever list the caller passed in. Here a crate of books is on its way to the North branch, and the program keeps the crates it sent in a set:

Java
// a crate of books on its way to a branch library
record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) {}

var titles = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma"));
var crate = new Crate("NORTH", titles);
var sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(crate));
titles.add("Ulysses");             // someone reuses their list
sent.contains(crate);              // false: the hashCode changed under the set
Kotlin
// a crate of books on its way to a branch library
data class Crate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>)

val titles = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma")
val crate = Crate("NORTH", titles)
val sent = hashSetOf(crate)
titles += "Ulysses"                // someone reuses their list
crate in sent                      // false: the hashCode changed under the set

The ShallowDemo in the Try it prints:

crate now:          Crate[branch=NORTH, titles=[Dune, Emma, Ulysses]]
hashCode changed:   true
sent.contains:      false

The crate is still in the set. The set just looks for it in the wrong place: a HashSet files each element under its hashCode, and that number changed after the crate was filed. Nothing threw. The fix is one line in the compact constructor:

Java
record SafeCrate(String branch, List<String> titles) {
    SafeCrate { titles = List.copyOf(titles); }          // an unmodifiable copy of the caller's list
}
Kotlin
data class SafeCrate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) {
    companion object {                                    // Kotlin can't reassign the parameter
        fun of(branch: String, titles: List<String>) = SafeCrate(branch, java.util.List.copyOf(titles))
    }
}

List.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy, and it throws NullPointerException for a null element, which is what you want for library data. Kotlin's List<String> is a read-only view, not an immutable list: the caller may still hold the same object as a MutableList. So a data class needs the same copy, made in a factory. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track made this point about threads. Here the cost is a lost crate, even with one thread.

A record is only as immutable as its components. Copy collections on the way in.

The last trap looks like a fix. To keep a member's phone number out of the logs, someone overrides the accessor, so phone() returns ****0123. The demo prints accessor: ****0123 and then toString: Masked[phone=01614960123]. The generated toString reads the field directly (those were the getters in the bootstrap arguments), so the logs never ask the accessor. The override breaks a promise in the Record Javadoc too: a copy built from the accessors, new Masked(m.phone()), should equal m, and the demo prints false. To hide a component, override toString itself, as the lab does.

Every slip is now checked at the counter and safe from other people's pens. Which leaves a fair question: how do you change one?

Run the Kotlin twin and look at the copy shares list line. Did copy() copy the list?

code.title: ShallowDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Equality, hashCode and toString are only as deep as the components. */ public class ShallowDemo { // a crate of books on its way to a branch library record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) {} record SafeCrate(String branch, List<String> titles) { SafeCrate { titles = List.copyOf(titles); } // unmodifiable copy } record Masked(String phone) { @Override public String phone() { return "****" + phone.substring(phone.length() - 4); } } record Rating(double stars) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> titles = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma")); Crate crate = new Crate("NORTH", titles); Set<Crate> sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(crate)); int before = crate.hashCode(); titles.add("Ulysses"); // someone reuses their list System.out.println("crate now: " + crate); System.out.println("hashCode changed: " + (before != crate.hashCode())); System.out.println("sent.contains: " + sent.contains(crate)); List<String> titles2 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma")); SafeCrate safe = new SafeCrate("SOUTH", titles2); titles2.add("Ulysses"); System.out.println("safe crate: " + safe); Masked m = new Masked("01614960123"); System.out.println("accessor: " + m.phone()); System.out.println("toString: " + m); System.out.println("copy equals orig: " + new Masked(m.phone()).equals(m)); System.out.println("NaN record equals: " + new Rating(Double.NaN).equals(new Rating(Double.NaN)) + " (but NaN == NaN is " + (Double.NaN == Double.NaN) + ")"); System.out.println("0.0 vs -0.0 equals: " + new Rating(0.0).equals(new Rating(-0.0)) + " (but 0.0 == -0.0 is " + (0.0 == -0.0) + ")"); } }

alt.title: ShallowDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // List<String> is a read-only view in Kotlin, not an immutable list: the caller may still hold a MutableList data class Crate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) // Kotlin can't reassign a constructor parameter, so the defensive copy goes in a factory data class SafeCrate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) { companion object { fun of(branch: String, titles: List<String>) = SafeCrate(branch, java.util.List.copyOf(titles)) } } data class Rating(val stars: Double) /** Equality, hashCode and toString are only as deep as the properties. */ fun main() { val titles = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma") val crate = Crate("NORTH", titles) val sent = hashSetOf(crate) val before = crate.hashCode() titles += "Ulysses" // someone reuses their list println("crate now: $crate") println("hashCode changed: ${before != crate.hashCode()}") println("sent.contains: ${crate in sent}") val copy = crate.copy(branch = "SOUTH") // copy() is shallow too titles += "Persuasion" println("copy shares list: $copy") val titles2 = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma") val safe = SafeCrate.of("SOUTH", titles2) titles2 += "Ulysses" println("safe crate: $safe") println("NaN data class ==: ${Rating(Double.NaN) == Rating(Double.NaN)} (but NaN == NaN is ${Double.NaN == Double.NaN})") println("0.0 vs -0.0 ==: ${Rating(0.0) == Rating(-0.0)} (but 0.0 == -0.0 is ${0.0 == -0.0})") }

try.expect: hashCode changed: true and sent.contains: false. After your fix the crate keeps its two titles, the hash code stays the same, and the set finds it. The masked record prints accessor: ****0123 but toString: Masked[phone=01614960123], and copy equals orig: false. The NaN records are equal and the 0.0 and -0.0 ones are not. In Kotlin, the copy shows Persuasion, which was added after the copy was made: copy() copies references, not the objects behind them.

sections.h: Changing a record: withers in Java, copy() in Kotlin
sections.html:
You don't change a stamped form. You fill in a new one, and it goes past the counter again. A renewal is exactly that: the same loan, with a new number of days. Kotlin generates copy() for this, with a named parameter for each property. Java generates nothing, so you write a wither, a method that returns a copy of the record with one component changed:

Java
record Loan(String memberId, int days, List<String> titles) {
    Loan {
        if (days <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("days must be positive: " + days);
        titles = List.copyOf(titles);
    }

    Loan withDays(int newDays) {                         // a wither, written by hand
        return new Loan(memberId, newDays, titles);      // through the canonical constructor
    }
}

Loan renewed = first.withDays(35);
Kotlin
data class LoanRequest(val memberId: String, val days: Int, val titles: List<String>) {
    init {
        require(days > 0) { "days must be positive: $days" }
    }
}

val renewed = first.copy(days = 35)                      // generated, and it runs init

Both go through the checks, and that's the point. The WitherDemo ends with wither ran the checks: days must be positive: -1, and its Kotlin twin with the same message from copy(), so there's no path to an invalid loan. Both also print same titles list object: true: a wither and copy() reuse the component references. That's safe here only because the record made its own unmodifiable copy at the counter.

The cost on the Java side is typing, and it grows with the record. In a 2020 design draft, Brian Goetz, Java's language architect, noted that a class has one getter per component but "could conceivably have O(2^n) withers". He asked that hand-written withers not become a best practice. Write withers only for the changes your domain really makes. A loan earns withDays; a shelfmark probably needs none.

A language fix exists on paper. JEP 468, derived record creation, proposes loan with { days = 35; }. It would take the record apart, run the block, and call the canonical constructor with the result. It's a Candidate JEP, no JDK has it, and in January 2026 Goetz wrote that it "has been 'on hold' for a while". Don't plan around it.

The other differences between the two languages matter more day to day. A data class may declare properties in its body, and Kotlin leaves those out of equals, hashCode, toString and copy(), so two objects that differ only there are equal. A record can't have body state at all. A data class can't be open, abstract or sealed, and a record is always final. Kotlin takes a data class apart with val (section, shelf) = mark, through generated componentN() functions. Java takes a record apart with record patterns, which lesson 3 of this track covers.

Where the two languages meet, Kotlin reads a Java record's accessors as properties, mark.section. @JvmRecord on a data class emits a real java.lang.Record, which Java code sees as one. The Kotlin docs warn that adding @JvmRecord to an existing class isn't a binary-compatible change, so decide when you create the class.

Records have one honest limit. A record can't hide its representation or keep any state beyond its components. A class that needs one private cache, or an inside different from its outside, falls back to writing all five places by hand. Goetz's design note on carrier classes, in Go deeper, sketches a way back.

try.title: Wither versus copy()
steps: Run WitherDemo and its twin WitherDemoKt. Compare the four lines each prints.
Add a withMemberId(String id) wither to the Java record and call it with " ". Should that be rejected? Add the check where every wither will get it.
In WitherDemo.kt, add var note = "" to the body of LoanRequest, set first.note = "renewed by phone", and print first == first.copy() and first.copy().note.

code.title: WitherDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java has no copy(): you write withers by hand, and each one calls the canonical constructor. */ public class WitherDemo { record Loan(String memberId, int days, List<String> titles) { Loan { if (days <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("days must be positive: " + days); titles = List.copyOf(titles); } Loan withDays(int newDays) { return new Loan(memberId, newDays, titles); } Loan withTitle(String extra) { var more = new ArrayList<>(titles); more.add(extra); return new Loan(memberId, days, more); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Loan first = new Loan("M-1042", 21, List.of("Dune")); Loan renewed = first.withDays(35).withTitle("Emma"); System.out.println("original: " + first); System.out.println("changed: " + renewed); System.out.println("same titles list object: " + (first.titles() == first.withDays(14).titles())); try { first.withDays(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither ran the checks: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: WitherDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // Kotlin generates copy(): one "wither" with a named, defaulted parameter per property data class LoanRequest(val memberId: String, val days: Int, val titles: List<String>) { init { require(days > 0) { "days must be positive: $days" } } } /** copy() runs init, and like a Java wither it copies references, not what they point to. */ fun main() { val first = LoanRequest("M-1042", 21, listOf("Dune")) val renewed = first.copy(days = 35, titles = first.titles + "Emma") println("original: $first") println("changed: $renewed") println("same titles list object: ${first.titles === first.copy(days = 14).titles}") try { first.copy(days = -1) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy ran the checks: ${e.message}") } }

try.expect: Both versions print the original loan, the renewed one with 35 days and two titles, same titles list object: true, and a rejected days must be positive: -1. Withers and copy() both reuse the component references, which is safe here only because the list can't change. The blank-id check belongs in the compact constructor, so every wither gets it for free. In Kotlin, first == first.copy() is true and the copy's note is empty: body properties are ignored by equals and not copied.

compare.title: A checked shelfmark in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Shelfmark.java
java.html: public record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { private static final Pattern SECTION = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}"); public Shelfmark { Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section"); section = section.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // tidy in place if (!SECTION.matcher(section).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad section: " + section); if (shelf < 1 || shelf > 999) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad shelf: " + shelf); } public Shelfmark next() { return new Shelfmark(section, shelf + 1); // past the counter again } }

kotlin.title: Shelfmark.kt
kotlin.html: data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) { init { require(SECTION.matches(section)) { "bad section: $section" } // can reject, can't tidy require(shelf in 1..999) { "bad shelf: $shelf" } } fun next() = Shelfmark(section, shelf + 1) // past init again companion object { private val SECTION = Regex("[A-Z]{3}") fun of(section: String, shelf: Int) = Shelfmark(section.trim().uppercase(), shelf) } }

compare.note: Both give you equals, hashCode and toString over all components, final fields, and a check that every construction goes through, including Kotlin's copy(). Three things differ. Java's compact constructor can tidy a parameter before it becomes a field; a data class can only reject it, so tidying lives in a factory and the public constructor stays open to raw input. Java deserialization rebuilds a record through its canonical constructor but skips a data class's init (@JvmRecord closes that gap). And Kotlin has copy() with named arguments, while Java has hand-written withers until JEP 468 ships, which it hasn't.

worked.title: Turn a hand-written membership form into a record

steps.say: When someone joins the library, the program fills in a membership form. Here it is as a JavaBean, a class with a getter and a setter for every field. It hands out its live list of branches, and its hand-written equals and toString weren't updated when the phone number was added. Any code can change a form after it was checked.
steps.code: public class MembershipForm { private String name; private String phone; private List<String> branches = new ArrayList<>(); public void setPhone(String phone) { this.phone = phone; } public List<String> getBranches() { return branches; } // hands out the live list // ... more setters and getters, and equals, hashCode, toString by hand }

alt.html: class MembershipForm { var name: String? = null var phone: String? = null val branches: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // hands out the live list }

steps.say: Write the header. The components are the whole state, and every setter is gone. Recompile: each place that called a setter is now a compile error, which is your list of code that changed a form after it was filled in.
steps.code: // 1. the components are the state public record MembershipForm(String name, PhoneNumber phone, List<String> branches) {}

alt.html: // 1. the properties are the state data class MembershipForm(val name: String, val phone: PhoneNumber, val branches: List<String>)

steps.say: Add the compact constructor. Reject what can't be valid, then copy the list so the caller can't change it later. phone is a PhoneNumber, the lab's record that checks itself, so the form doesn't repeat those checks.
steps.code: public record MembershipForm(String name, PhoneNumber phone, List<String> branches) { public MembershipForm { Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name"); // 2. reject Objects.requireNonNull(phone, "phone"); if (name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("blank name"); branches = List.copyOf(branches); // 3. copy if (branches.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no home branch"); } }

alt.html: data class MembershipForm(val name: String, val phone: PhoneNumber, val branches: List<String>) { init { require(name.isNotBlank()) { "blank name" } // 2. reject require(branches.isNotEmpty()) { "no home branch" } } companion object { fun of(name: String, phone: PhoneNumber, branches: List<String>) = MembershipForm(name, phone, java.util.List.copyOf(branches)) // 3. copy } }

steps.say: Add only the wither the library needs. Members do change their phone numbers, so withPhone earns its place. It calls the canonical constructor, so a changed form can't skip the checks. In Kotlin, copy(phone = ...) already exists and runs init.
steps.code: // 4. one wither, through the canonical constructor public MembershipForm withPhone(PhoneNumber newPhone) { return new MembershipForm(name, newPhone, branches); }

alt.html: // 4. no wither to write: copy() is generated and runs init val updated = form.copy(phone = PhoneNumber("0161 496 0999"))

drill.title: A checked member number from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write record MemberId(String value) that rejects null, trims and upper-cases the value, and then rejects anything that isn't M- followed by four to six digits. Then write the Kotlin version. Which of the two can store the tidied value without a factory?

answer.html: public record MemberId(String value) { private static final Pattern SHAPE = Pattern.compile("M-[0-9]{4,6}"); public MemberId { Objects.requireNonNull(value, "value"); value = value.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // tidy first if (!SHAPE.matcher(value).matches()) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad member id: " + value); } } }

alt.html: data class MemberId(val value: String) { init { require(SHAPE.matches(value)) { "bad member id: $value" } // can reject, can't tidy } companion object { private val SHAPE = Regex("M-[0-9]{4,6}") fun of(raw: String) = MemberId(raw.trim().uppercase()) // so tidying lives here } }

recap: A record is a final class whose header lists its components. javac writes private final fields, accessors, one canonical constructor, and equals, hashCode and toString from that list, so they can't drift apart.

Check and tidy in the compact constructor. Every path goes through it: new, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization. Kotlin's init is the twin, but it can't tidy a parameter, and Java deserialization skips it unless the class is @JvmRecord.
Equality compares every component: Objects.equals for references and compare for primitives, so NaN equals NaN and 0.0 doesn't equal -0.0. Arrays compare by reference.

Records are only shallowly immutable. Copy collection components with List.copyOf, or a changed list loses its record in a HashSet. The generated methods read fields, not accessors, so hide a secret in toString.
Kotlin generates copy(); Java has hand-written withers, because JEP 468 is on hold and in no JDK.
The limit: a record can't keep state beyond its components or hide its representation, and it's still an identity object. A class that needs a private cache goes back to writing everything by hand.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our MemberCard(String phone, List<String> branches) record is immutable, so it's safe to keep in a HashSet and to log as it is." Explain, in your own words, the two ways that can go wrong and what you would change.
explain.answer: A record is only shallowly immutable. Its fields can't be reassigned, but branches points to whatever list the caller passed in, and if the caller keeps changing that list, the record's hashCode changes and the set can't find it any more. I'd copy the list in the compact constructor with List.copyOf. Logging is the second problem: the generated toString prints every component, so the member's full phone number goes into the logs. Overriding the phone() accessor doesn't help, because toString reads the field directly. I'd override toString and print only the last four digits there, or better, make the phone a PhoneNumber record that masks itself.

deeper.html:
Two details round out the picture.

A Java record can't hide its canonical constructor. The Record Javadoc says it "must provide at least as much access as the record class", and javac enforces it:

Java
public record Key(String v) { private Key { } }
// error: invalid canonical constructor in record Key
//   (attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public)
Kotlin
data class Key private constructor(val v: String) {
    companion object { fun of(raw: String) = Key(raw.trim()) }
}
// warning (Kotlin 2.4): non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method

So in Java, the checks must live inside the constructor, where nobody can bypass them. Kotlin lets you make a data class constructor private and send callers through a factory that tidies, but copy() still exposes it. Kotlin 2.4.21 warns about this, says the warning becomes an error in language version 2.5, and offers @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor.

The second detail is about what comes after records. In a January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", Brian Goetz describes the cliff you fall off when a class is almost a record: one derived field or one private cache, and you're back to writing everything by hand. The note sketches carrier classes, written like class Point(int x, int y) { ... }: a normal class with a record-style state description. The language would require the canonical constructor and the accessors and give the class a deconstruction pattern, while the class declares its own fields and need not be final. It's a design note, and no JEP exists yet, so treat it as a direction for now.
